today.label: Today
today.description: The system as Hickel describes it: capital decides what is produced, votes stop at the political layer, and the North depends on cheap labor and nature from the South.

alt.label: Democratic socialism
alt.description: Hickel's proposed transformation: democracy extended into production through a decommodified social foundation, a public finance mechanism, workplace democracy and a job guarantee, with no need for an imperial arrangement.

lenses.title: Two layers of decision-making
lenses.question: Why doesn't democracy in politics mean democracy in the economy? Who decides what gets produced?

lenses.title: The law of value
lenses.question: Why does capital keep investing in fossil fuels when renewables are cheaper?

lenses.title: Planning: elite vs democratic
lenses.question: Who plans the economy today, and what would replace that?

lenses.title: North ← South
lenses.question: How are cheap labor and cheap nature taken from the Global South, and how is that arrangement enforced?

lenses.title: Ecosystem
lenses.question: How do extraction and pollution fit into the system, and why must total energy use fall in rich countries?

lenses.title: Scales of society
lenses.question: Which decisions belong at the neighborhood, firm, national and global levels?

nodes.label: Citizens / voters
nodes.description: People who vote in political elections but have no say over what the economy produces.

byState.alt: People whose vote reaches both politics and production: setting investment goals, running workplaces and deciding local budgets.

sources.note: We live in political democracies, but there is no democracy in the system of production.

nodes.label: Government / state
nodes.description: Issues the currency and controls the military. Hickel calls it neutral: it does whatever those who control it decide, and today that is capital.

byState.alt: The state under democratic control: it uses its power as currency issuer to fund what people vote for, limited only by real resources (inflation).

sources.note: The state is captured by capital; its spending clears the way for profit.
As a currency issuer, the state has no financial limit on funding what's needed; the real limit is inflation.

sources.anchor: the capitalist class is in power
sources.note: The capitalist class is in power, and governments align with its interests.

nodes.label: Media
nodes.description: Owned by billionaires. It spreads the 'common sense' that capitalism equals freedom, and campaigns against socialist candidates.

sources.note: Democracy can't work when billionaires own the press and fund campaigns.
'Capitalism is freedom' is a textbook case of Gramscian cultural hegemony.

nodes.label: Military
nodes.description: Receives huge public budgets while public services are cut, and is used to keep the Global South 'cheap'.

sources.note: Public money flows to the military, police and surveillance instead of public services.
The military-industrial complex and the wars waged by core economies.

nodes.label: Mass-based party
nodes.description: A party rooted in working-class communities that can win elections and use state power. Hickel argues protest alone is not enough.

sources.note: Climate protest has built public will but lacks the political power to transform the system.

sources.anchor: building some kind of political machine
sources.note: What's needed is a mass-based party that can win elections.

sources.anchor: deep roots in working class communities
sources.note: A mass party with deep roots in working-class communities is the objective, and new vehicles may be needed where existing parties will not serve.
A movement tied to one figure is vulnerable; the answer is real mass parties with broad leadership.

nodes.label: Neighborhood associations
nodes.description: The movement's ground game: local organizations that build trust and the political understanding to withstand media backlash. They also decide on local job guarantee budgets.

sources.note: Build neighborhood associations so people can resist media smears; going door to door isn't enough.
The job guarantee can be decentralized all the way down to neighborhoods.

nodes.label: Workers (North)
nodes.description: Their labor produces the surplus, but they have no say over how it is reinvested. They are kept in line by the threat of unemployment.

byState.alt: Workers with guaranteed employment and a say in their workplaces, so their bargaining power rises.

sources.note: The surplus comes from our labor, so we should have a say in how it's invested.
The threat of unemployment keeps workers subordinate to their bosses.

nodes.label: Capital
nodes.description: Private banks, big firms and the 1% who own most investable wealth. They control production and direct it toward whatever is most profitable.

byState.alt: Still present, but taxed so that it has less command over society's labor, and no longer in charge of what society produces.

sources.note: A small elite (big banks, major firms, the 1%) controls production and decides what gets made.
Wealth matters because money is command over other people's labor.

nodes.label: Investment & planning
nodes.description: Where society's surplus is reinvested, and the corporate plans that steer it. Planning already happens in boardrooms and banks; it is just undemocratic. The capitalist law of value filters it: profitability, not need or cost, decides. In the alternative, the public finance mechanism takes this role.

sources.note: The capitalist law of value makes profitability the main test for investment, so allocation is irrational.
The capitalist economy is already planned, inside the big firms.
Corporations literally make 5- and 10-year plans; the problem is that the planning is undemocratic.

sources.anchor: made in the city of London
sources.note: Decisions about what happens in the nation are made in the City of London, where the surplus is concentrated.

sources.anchor: commercial banks and the big investment firms
sources.note: Investment happens overwhelmingly through commercial banks and big investment firms, aiming at short-term profit.

nodes.label: Productive capacity
nodes.description: Labor, engineers, factories and resources: the real economy. Hickel stresses that the stock market is not the economy.

sources.anchor: stock market is not the economy
sources.note: The real economy is goods, services, labor and resources, not the stock market.
sources.quote: the stock market is not the economy

sources.anchor: capitalism does not give us technologies
sources.note: Workers and engineers create technologies such as AI; capital only controls how they're used.

nodes.label: Necessary goods & services
nodes.description: In chronic short supply because they are less profitable, even in the richest economies.

byState.alt: Pillar 1: a decommodified social foundation with universal access, produced because it is needed.

sources.note: Luxuries are overproduced while public transit, nutritious food and affordable housing are in chronic short supply.
Pillar 1: organize production to guarantee healthcare, education, housing, energy and water for all.

sources.anchor: increases the bargaining power of the working class
sources.note: Decommodified basics raise the bargaining power of the working class.
In the US, half the population cannot afford the health care they need, despite massive production.
No amount of willingness to pay gets capital to build public transit where it is not profitable.

nodes.label: Less-necessary production
nodes.description: Highly profitable, energy-intensive output that adds little to wellbeing, including products designed to break.

byState.alt: Deliberately scaled down, which frees labor and resources for necessities and keeps public spending non-inflationary.

sources.note: Mansions, private jets, SUVs, fast fashion and weapons are overproduced.
Phones, laptops and fast fashion are designed to break or go out of style.
SUVs, fast fashion, mansions, private jets and cruise ships overwhelmingly benefit a small fraction of society.

nodes.label: Fossil fuels
nodes.description: More expensive than renewables but three to four times more profitable, so capital keeps investing in them.

byState.alt: Phased out as public finance builds renewable capacity directly.

sources.anchor: three or four times more profitable
sources.note: Fossil fuels are 3–4× more profitable than renewables, so capital invests in them.
BlackRock dropped its climate commitments because the green transition wasn't profitable enough.
Renewables are a competitive, low-barrier sector; fossil fuels allow monopoly power.
Capital already sunk into fossil infrastructure wants to keep using it.

nodes.label: Renewable energy
nodes.description: Cheaper than fossil fuels and already available, but underinvested because it is less profitable.

byState.alt: Built quickly through public finance; China's lead in renewables is the example.

sources.note: Renewables are cheaper than fossil fuels but less profitable.
China used public finance and became the world leader in renewables.
China installs more renewable capacity each year than the rest of the world combined.

sources.anchor: public control over the financial system
sources.note: It can do this because it has public control over its financial system.

nodes.label: Threat of unemployment
nodes.description: An artificial scarcity: workers wait until capital finds it profitable to hire them. It also blocks any conversation about scaling down harmful industries.

sources.note: Unemployment and the fear of it are a main source of misery and insecurity.

nodes.label: Public finance mechanism
nodes.description: Pillar 2: public investment toward democratically ratified goals such as climate mitigation, ecological regeneration and affordable housing, without waiting for capital.

sources.anchor: public finance mechanism that can make
sources.note: A public finance mechanism invests in what people vote for, and quickly.

nodes.label: Democratic workplaces
nodes.description: Pillar 3: workers decide what to produce, for whose benefit, and how to share what their labor yields.

sources.note: Workplace democracy: workers decide what their firm produces and how the yields are shared.
Worker-owned firms like Mondragon set their own wage ratios, which keeps inequality low.
Workers who took over an Italian car plant switched it to cargo bikes and solar panels.
Mondragon in Spain is worker-owned and worker-run, despite competitive pressures from operating under capitalism.
Workers elect their managers and collectively set pay ratios such as 1 to 4 or 1 to 6.
Yugoslavia was a market socialist economy in which workers controlled production.

examples: pay ratios of 1 to 4 or 1 to 6

nodes.label: Public job guarantee
nodes.description: Anyone can train and work on socially necessary projects (renewables, transit, retrofits, ecosystem regeneration) at a living wage. This ends unemployment and raises the standard for private employers.

sources.note: The job guarantee polls at around 80%.
It raises labor's bargaining power and moves capacity toward social goals.

nodes.label: Neighborhood job budget
nodes.description: Public money given to neighborhoods, which decide democratically what work is needed locally, such as a community garden, a gym, elder care or a kids' soccer team.

sources.note: Neighborhoods collectively decide what to invest work in.

nodes.label: National projects & commanding heights
nodes.description: Large projects such as a national rail system, plus public control of strategic sectors (energy, rail), decided centrally. Each task is decided at the level that suits it.

sources.note: Big projects like national rail need centralized decision-making.

sources.anchor: public control over the commanding heights
sources.note: Strategic sectors like energy and rail should be under public control.
Different forms of production need different levels of decentralization.

nodes.label: Global South states
nodes.description: States that try to organize their own resources and production for their people's needs are attacked through coups, wars or debt.

byState.alt: Sovereign development: free to organize their productive capacity around their people's needs.

sources.note: Any country that starts on sovereign development gets attacked.
Global South liberation struggles (e.g. the Sahel today, China historically) are what drive world-historical change.
The South needs a second stage of decolonization: reclaiming control of its productive capacities.

nodes.label: Workers (South)
nodes.description: 'Cheap labor': low wages, and in some cases forced labor, feeding Northern supply chains.

byState.alt: Labor organized around national development and their own wellbeing.

sources.note: Capital accumulation needs cheap labor and cheap nature (Jason Moore's terms).
Slave labor in Congo is part of the supply chains behind our technologies.

nodes.label: People of the South
nodes.description: The people of the periphery, where deprivation is most extreme. Sanctions, structural adjustment, coups and wars aimed at their governments land on them: public services like health care and education cut, development blocked, shortages, mass death. So does most of the climate damage.

byState.alt: With sovereign development, production is organized around their needs: good for the workers and the people of the South.

sources.anchor: Deprivation is obviously most extreme in the periphery
sources.note: Deprivation is most extreme in the periphery, where imperialist appropriation perpetuates poverty.

sources.anchor: the mass death that's been imposed on that population
sources.note: Mass death has been imposed on the population of Gaza.
Under sanctions, structural adjustment or invasion, a country cannot mobilize production for its people's needs.

sources.anchor: for the workers and the people of the south
sources.note: Sovereign development is good for the workers and the people of the South.
More than 2 billion people live in food insecurity, and billions lack basics that are easy to produce.
There is no reason people across the South could not live as long as people in Spain or Switzerland.

examples: public services cut under structural adjustment
more than 2 billion in food insecurity

nodes.label: Land & resources (South)
nodes.description: 'Cheap nature': raw materials taken with no regard for regulation, dispossession or the people who depend on them.

sources.note: Colonies were organized to supply cheap nature and cheap labor.

nodes.label: Ecosystems & atmosphere
nodes.description: The shared material base of North and South alike. All production draws on it and dumps into it, and under growth, efficiency gains get wiped out by rising total use. Its degradation does not land evenly.

byState.alt: Total energy and material use falls in rich countries, so ecosystems can regenerate.

sources.note: To meet the Paris goals, high-income countries must cut total energy use.
Efficiency gains (e.g. from AI) get wiped out by growth in total use.
Rich countries overshot their fair shares and effectively colonized the atmospheric commons.

nodes.label: Waste from throwaway goods
nodes.description: Phones, laptops, fridges and fast fashion are designed to break down or go out of style, so we keep replacing them. Hickel calls planned obsolescence great for capitalists' profits but devastating for the climate and the environment.

byState.alt: Built to last: longer-lasting products are possible, and with workers deciding what gets made, unnecessary production can be scaled down.

sources.anchor: designed to break down after a short period of time
sources.note: Smartphones, laptops and fridges are designed to break down so we have to keep buying new ones.

sources.anchor: planned obsolescence is capital does that
sources.note: Capital uses planned obsolescence because it is profitable, even though it is against our interests.
Unnecessary pollution, environmental harm, and products that die after two years due to planned obsolescence.

sources.anchor: possible to develop longer lasting products
sources.note: Longer-lasting products are possible; capital doesn't invest in them because they are less profitable.

nodes.label: Core monopolies
nodes.description: Northern firms' monopolies over intellectual property, high technology and capital goods. Because everyone needs these goods, their prices can be set high, which forces the South to export more of its cheapened output to pay for them. Capital tends toward monopoly in general, because it removes competitive pressure. Hickel treats cloud capital’s feudal-looking features as an outflow of capitalism, not a departure from it.

sources.anchor: monopoly power over um over certain advanced sectors
sources.note: Western monopoly power over advanced sectors is central to its development model.
Northern firms turned to monopolizing intellectual property and high-tech production.
Capital tends toward monopoly because it removes competitive pressure; cloud capital is an outflow of capitalism, not a departure from it.

nodes.label: IMF / World Bank
nodes.description: After the Volcker shock tipped the South into a debt crisis, the IMF and World Bank imposed structural adjustment: privatize, cut public services, abolish industrial policy, and stop financing development with your own currency. Hickel calls neoliberalism the mechanism that restored the imperial arrangement.

sources.note: Structural adjustment forced privatization, service cuts and the end of industrial policy.

sources.anchor: mechanism for restoring the imperial arrangement
sources.note: Neoliberalism was the mechanism for restoring the imperial arrangement.

sources.anchor: curtailed the ability of states to issue national currency
sources.note: It curtailed states’ ability to use their own currency and public finance.

nodes.label: Dollar system (petrodollar)
nodes.description: Oil is traded in dollars, which creates constant demand for the dollar and lets the US import freely and run deficits. A switch to renewables, or to oil sold in other currencies, threatens that privilege.

sources.note: The petrodollar is a core pillar of US imperial privilege.

sources.anchor: in currencies that are not the US dollar
sources.note: Selling oil in currencies other than the dollar undermines Western capital accumulation.

nodes.label: Far right
nodes.description: When capital squeezes its own workers and no socialist movement exists to channel their anger, the far right captures it with anti-elite rhetoric, a fake revolution whose beneficiaries are the same capitalist class.

sources.note: When the crisis comes and no alternative has been built, we get fascism.
The right offers a fake revolution that ultimately backs the existing capitalist class.
Fascists take control and create social chaos.

nodes.label: Liberal parties
nodes.description: Committed to rights in principle, but to capitalist control of production first. They go as far as they can without touching ownership, fail to resolve the underlying contradictions, and so keep the seat warm for the next right-wing government.

sources.note: Liberal parties effectively keep the seat warm for the next right-wing party.
Liberals will go as far as they can without addressing control over production.
Liberalism resolves conflicts between rights and capital in favor of capital.
US elections move power between two corporate-backed parties, both capitalist.

nodes.label: China & South–South cooperation
nodes.description: Already a counter-force today: China's rising wages and its break into Western monopolies pinch core profits, while the Belt and Road, swap lines and BRICS let Southern countries get technology and trade on fairer terms, outside the dollar. China is still a peripheral economy, losing value and resources to the core. It has public control over finance and the commanding heights, but Hickel says it lacks worker control over production.

byState.alt: South–South trade, finance and defense cooperation that lets every Southern state delink from the imperial core.

sources.note: Chinese manufacturing wages have risen many times over since 2005.
The Belt and Road builds trade infrastructure within the Global South.
Swap lines allow trade without the dollar or the euro.
China is still peripheral in GDP per capita and suffers a massive outflow of value and resources to the core.
China’s public control over finance and the commanding heights directs investment toward national plans; Hickel says worker control is what is lacking.

sources.anchor: very high levels of democracy perception
sources.note: Hickel cites the Democracy Perception Index, which he calls a Western NGO: around 80% in China say they live in a democracy.

nodes.label: Credit guidance
nodes.description: Rules the democratic state sets for commercial banks: limit lending to fossil fuels and other damaging industries, and meet quotas for renewables, rail and other democratically chosen goals. Finance subordinated to democratic objectives.

sources.note: A credit guidance framework steers bank credit away from fossil fuels and toward renewables.

sources.anchor: imposes rules on the commercial banks
sources.note: Credit guidance imposes investment rules and quotas on commercial banks.
A credit guidance system organizes investment toward the most necessary sectors.
In the mid-20th century, governments told commercial banks what they could not fund and what they must.
Credit guidance, industrial policy and public finance have been hollowed out since the 1980s.

nodes.label: Southern public finance & industrial policy
nodes.description: Any state that issues its own currency can fund what it needs: houses, schools, clinics, sanitation, regenerative farming, and jobs for people capital leaves unemployed. Industrial policy builds a sovereign industrial base.

sources.note: A government that issues its own currency can finance whatever its labor and materials allow.
Train and hire the hundreds of millions left unemployed because capital finds them unprofitable.

nodes.label: Capital in the South
nodes.description: Capitalists in the periphery. A capitalist in the core can concede to workers and get cheap labor elsewhere; in the periphery there is no elsewhere, so Hickel says the option left is violent repression. National capital organizes Southern production for its own profit alongside foreign capital, which largely controls it, and some Southern ruling classes benefit from Western capital arrangements.

sources.anchor: if you're a capitalist in the periphery
sources.note: A capitalist in the periphery has nowhere else to get cheap labor, so cannot concede to workers’ demands.
A capitalist society in the periphery has no alternative but to suppress these demands.
Southern production is determined by national capital for its own profit, and also by foreign capital.
The South’s productive capacities are largely controlled by Western capital.
In some core BRICS members, ruling classes benefit from Western capital arrangements.

nodes.label: AI & automation
nodes.description: Hickel calls the problems with AI a symptom of capitalism. Capital controls the technology and deploys it for profit, so people whose jobs are automated are cut off. The problem is not the technology but the system it is deployed under.

byState.alt: With democratic say over how it is deployed, reduced labor time is a benefit: a shorter working week for everyone, or labor moved to ecological restoration, care work and public transit.

sources.anchor: the problems we see with AI are a symptom
sources.note: The problems seen with AI are a symptom of the problems of capitalism.
The problem is not the technology but the system under which it is deployed.

sources.anchor: What capital does is it controls them
sources.note: Workers and engineers create technologies; capital controls them and decides how they are used.

nodes.label: Social movements & protest
nodes.description: Labor, feminist, anti-imperialist and climate movements. Democracy, public services, the weekend and women’s rights all had to be fought for against the capitalist class. Hickel argues protest has limits, and that these struggles share objectives a mass party could unite.

sources.note: Progress is never handed down by capital; it is fought for by struggles from below.

sources.anchor: objectives of the labor movement are the same
sources.note: The labor, feminist, anti-imperialist and climate movements share objectives.

nodes.label: UN Security Council
nodes.description: Its permanent members can veto anything the UN tries to do that they find unacceptable. Mearsheimer says it was set up to protect great powers from decisions they don’t like. Finkelstein adds that a veto can also go unused when a threat hangs over a vote. Russia and China hold the veto too; this map draws only the North’s state.

sources.anchor: set up to protect great powers
sources.note: The Security Council was set up to protect great powers from rules or decisions they don’t like.
The UN is ultimately a political institution, responsive to political pressures.
Veto holders can hold back under threat, for fear of being blamed for what follows.

nodes.label: UN General Assembly
nodes.description: Virtually every state sits here, and the South has the majority. Hickel: the G77 used that democratic majority to pass the New International Economic Order in 1974. Mearsheimer: the power that counts sits in the Security Council.

sources.anchor: where they held a democratic majority
sources.note: The G77 cooperated in the UN, where it held a democratic majority.
The General Assembly includes virtually all the states in the UN.

nodes.label: International Court of Justice
nodes.description: The UN’s legal arm. A state can bring a case against another and win interim orders long before the full case is decided. Finkelstein calls a top court the “condensation of all the politics” in the world, though he admits he wrongly expected this one would never rule against a Western ally. Varoufakis says its job is to hold states to account, including those who aid and abet.

sources.anchor: legal arm of the United Nations
sources.note: The ICJ is the legal arm of the UN.
The highest court is a condensation of all the politics of the world.

sources.anchor: I couldn't have been more wrong
sources.note: He expected a court with powerful members would never rule as it did, and says he was wrong.

sources.anchor: hold the rest of us into
sources.note: The job of the ICC and ICJ is to hold others to account for aiding and abetting.
sources.speaker: Varoufakis

nodes.label: International Criminal Court
nodes.description: Set up by treaty, not a UN organ, and it charges individual leaders rather than states. Varoufakis: it can’t enforce much, but even a small chance of a Nuremberg-style trial instills real fear in strongmen; Western leaders applaud some indictments and shrug off others; and it should tell leaders who supply arms that they are personally culpable. Rifkind warns that charging a leader mid-war may give them a reason to prolong it.

sources.note: Even a small probability of a Nuremberg-style trial instills fear in strongmen.
sources.speaker: Varoufakis

sources.note: The ICC should tell leaders who arm a belligerent that they are personally culpable.
sources.speaker: Varoufakis

sources.anchor: prolong that war rather than face justice
sources.note: Declaring a leader a war criminal mid-war risks them prolonging the war.
sources.speaker: Rifkind

flows.label: votes
flows.description: Elections decide who governs.

sources.note: We have political democracy.

flows.label: no vote over production
flows.description: Votes never reach decisions about what gets produced and for whose benefit. Those stay with capital.

sources.note: Capitalism is fundamentally anti-democratic: we have zero say over production.
The answer is to extend democracy into the realm of production (Eugene Debs).
“Voting with your dollars” gives the rich far more votes, and unprofitable needs still do not get produced.

sources.anchor: not even a shadow of democracy
sources.note: In the system of production, not even a shadow of democracy is allowed.

flows.label: capture
flows.description: Capital controls the state through campaign finance and influence, so state spending serves profit.

sources.note: The state is totally captured by capital.
Billionaires buy politicians openly through campaign finance.
Corporations and billionaires buy off politicians and so effectively determine political outcomes.
A 2014 study Hickel cites found US policy follows the preferences of elites, not the majority.

sources.anchor: only about half of the population
sources.note: Hickel cites the Democracy Perception Index: in the US, France and the UK only about half believe they live in a real democracy.

flows.label: ownership
flows.description: Billionaires own the press.

sources.note: Billionaires own our press.
Billionaires, corporations and foreign oligarchs own UK media, so discussion is mediated through corporate media.

flows.label: 'capitalism = freedom'
flows.description: Cultural hegemony gets people to accept a system that works against their interests as natural and good.

sources.note: 'Capitalism is freedom' is cultural hegemony.

flows.label: labor
flows.description: Workers spend 8 hours a day, for their whole working lives, in a production system they don't control.

sources.note: Production shapes our time, our cities and our future, and we have no say.
Production decides what we do with our time as workers, 8 hours a day, for our entire working lives.

flows.label: surplus
flows.description: The surplus that workers generate is captured by capital.

sources.note: The surplus we generate is reinvested without our say.

flows.label: law of value
flows.description: The capitalist law of value: investment goes to the most profitable option, whatever it costs society.

sources.note: Overcome the capitalist law of value that makes profitability the investment rule.

sources.anchor: producing what is most profitable to capital
sources.note: Production and finance are organized around what is most profitable to capital, not what is needed.

sources.anchor: Climate change is a class war
sources.note: Investment follows profit for capital, not necessity for humanity.
A billionaire who owns an investment firm can channel vast amounts of our surplus wherever they like.

flows.label: heavy investment
flows.description: Fossil fuels get the money because they are 3–4× more profitable.

sources.anchor: three or four times more profitable
sources.note: Capital invests in fossil fuels because they're 3–4× more profitable.
sources.quote: three or four times more profitable than renewables

sources.note: BlackRock abandoned its climate rules to return to traditional profit sectors.

flows.label: inadequate investment
flows.description: Renewables are cheaper, but they get too little investment because they are less profitable.

sources.note: Renewables are cheaper but less profitable.

flows.label: overproduction
flows.description: Profitable luxuries are overproduced.

sources.note: Massive overproduction of mansions, jets, SUVs, fast fashion and weapons.

sources.anchor: massive overproduction of things like SUVs
sources.note: Capital overproduces things like SUVs and fast fashion.

flows.label: chronic shortage
flows.description: Necessities are underproduced because they are less profitable.

sources.note: Chronic shortages of transit, nutritious food and affordable housing.
Affordable housing, renewable energy and longer-lasting products are chronically underproduced because they are not profitable.

flows.label: discipline
flows.description: The fear of losing your job keeps workers obedient.

sources.note: Disobey and you're replaced.

flows.label: military spending
flows.description: Public money goes into weapons, which transfers surplus to the billionaires who own the arms industry.

sources.note: Money for the military, police and surveillance, not for public services.
The arms industry is an example of the state transferring surplus to billionaires.

flows.label: coups & wars
flows.description: Countries that pursue sovereign development are bombed, or their governments toppled, to make them 'cheap' again.

sources.anchor: inflationary for capital in the core
sources.note: Sovereign development raises input prices for capital in the core, so it gets attacked.
The US has carried out dozens of regime-change operations in the Global South.
The US carried out around 70 regime-change operations in the Global South.
The states targeted are the ones trying to set their own development path.
Thomas Sankara was assassinated in a French-backed coup and replaced by a dictator who served the West for decades.

flows.label: sanctions
flows.description: Governments that seek sovereign development are sanctioned, often straight away: Hickel's examples include almost every socialist government of the 20th century, China after its revolution, and Cuba today.

sources.anchor: they sanctioned almost all of the socialist governments
sources.note: The West sanctioned almost all socialist governments of the 20th century soon after they formed.
After its revolution China was immediately sanctioned, to strangle the development of its economy.

sources.anchor: is being strangled right now by US sanctions
sources.note: Cuba is being strangled by US sanctions.

flows.label: public services cut, development blocked
flows.description: The pressure on a government lands on its people. Structural adjustment forced Southern governments to cut public services, privatize public industries and resources, and abandon industrial policy, and extreme poverty rose sharply during this forced liberalization in the 1990s. Under sanctions a state cannot mobilize production for its people's needs: Hickel attributes the shortages socialist countries suffered to blockades and sanctions. Meanwhile labor that could staff hospitals and schools in the South is kept making export goods for Northern firms.

sources.note: Structural adjustment forced governments to privatize public industries and resources, cut public services and abolish industrial policy.

sources.anchor: extreme poverty increased dramatically during the period of forced liberalization
sources.note: On a basic-needs poverty line, extreme poverty increased dramatically during the forced liberalization of the 1990s.
Under sanctions, structural adjustment or invasion, a country cannot mobilize production to meet its people's needs.

sources.anchor: due to the blockades and sanctions
sources.note: Shortages in socialist countries were due to blockades and sanctions.

sources.anchor: staff hospitals and schools in the global south
sources.note: The South's drained labor could staff hospitals and schools at home; instead it makes tech gadgets and fast fashion for Northern firms.
As public services are slashed, people’s lives get harder.

flows.label: bombing & invasion
flows.description: Wars kill civilians directly. Hickel cites the US bombing of North Korea, which destroyed some 85% of its structures and killed a huge share of its people, and places today's attacks on Palestine, Iran, Venezuela and Cuba in the same pattern of Western intervention.

sources.note: US bombing destroyed about 85% of North Korea's structures and killed a huge portion of the population.

sources.anchor: never ending process of of brutal western intervention
sources.note: Palestine, Iran, Lebanon, Venezuela, Cuba: a never-ending process of brutal Western intervention.

sources.anchor: the mass death that's been imposed on that population
sources.note: Mass death has been imposed on the population of Gaza.

flows.label: production for people's needs
flows.description: With sovereignty, a Southern state can organize production around its own population's needs. A sovereign currency can fund schools, clinics, housing and sanitation, and in Hickel's comparison of states in the periphery at the same income level, socialist states did better than capitalist ones on infant mortality, life expectancy, health care and education.

sources.anchor: building houses, schools, clinics, sanitation systems
sources.note: A state issuing its own currency can fund houses, schools, clinics, sanitation and public services.

sources.anchor: socialist states outperformed the capitalist states
sources.note: Across 15 indicators (infant mortality, life expectancy, health care, education…), socialist states in the periphery outperformed capitalist ones at the same GDP per capita.

sources.anchor: schools and sanitation systems for their own population
sources.note: Resources go into sweatshop goods for Northern brands instead of hospitals, schools and sanitation for the country's own population.

sources.anchor: for the workers and the people of the south
sources.note: Sovereign development is good for the workers and the people of the South.
Degrowth targets the core; Southern countries under-consume and need growth in infrastructure and industry for human needs.

flows.label: embodied labor drain
flows.description: Growth and consumption in the core depend on labor appropriated from the South through unequal exchange.

sources.note: Core growth depends on massive appropriation of labor from the South.
For every unit of embodied labor the South imports, it exports many times more.

sources.anchor: half of total consumption in the core
sources.note: Around half of core consumption of materials and labor is net-appropriated from the South.
Production happens disproportionately in China and the South, while profits and surplus accumulate in the North.

flows.label: embodied resource drain
flows.description: Raw materials, land and energy flow from South to North, priced cheaply.

sources.note: …and appropriation of nature from the South.

flows.label: extraction
flows.description: Growth-driven material and energy throughput.

sources.note: Rich countries need to scale down total energy use.

sources.anchor: four times over the sustainable boundary
sources.note: Rich countries’ total material consumption is something like four times the sustainable boundary.

flows.label: emissions
flows.description: Burning fossil fuels drives the climate crisis.

sources.anchor: three or four times more profitable
sources.note: Investing in fossil fuels even as the world burns.

flows.label: pollution & waste
flows.description: Energy-intensive, unnecessary production, including products built to break.

sources.note: Capital will never voluntarily cut production of things that are profitable.
sources.quote: Capital will never voluntarily reduce production of things that are profitable.

flows.label: built to break, replaced
flows.description: Products are designed to break down or go out of style after a short time, so people have to keep buying new ones: profitable for capital, against our interests.

sources.anchor: planned obsolescence is capital does that
sources.note: Capital uses planned obsolescence because it is profitable, even though it is against our interests.

sources.anchor: designed to break down after a short period of time
sources.note: Smartphones, laptops and fridges are designed to break down so we have to keep buying new ones.

flows.label: environmental harm
flows.description: Hickel calls this throwaway cycle devastating for the climate and the environment: unnecessary pollution and environmental harm.

sources.anchor: devastating for climate and the environment
sources.note: Built-to-break products are amazing for profits but devastating for climate and the environment.
Unnecessary pollution, environmental harm, and products that die after two years due to planned obsolescence.

flows.label: e-waste shipped South
flows.description: Discarded electronics are shipped from richer to poorer countries, much of it uncontrolled and undocumented. Informal recycling there exposes workers, children and neighbouring communities to hazardous substances. This arrow does not come from Hickel's talks; it rests on ITU/UNITAR and WHO.

flows.label: profits
flows.description: Fossil fuel profits flow back to capital, which then has even more to invest by the same rule. This closes the accumulation loop.

sources.note: Capital pours investment into the profit sectors: fossil fuels, SUVs, fast fashion, weapons.

sources.anchor: three or four times more profitable
sources.note: Fossil fuels pay 3–4× more than renewables.

flows.label: profits
flows.description: Profits from luxuries and products built to break return to capital, funding more of the same.

sources.note: Capital's investments make the social and ecological crises worse instead of solving them.
Planned obsolescence is done because it's profitable.

flows.label: arms profits
flows.description: Military spending moves public surplus into the pockets of those who own the weapons industry.

sources.note: The weapons industry channels our surplus to billionaires.

flows.label: hires only if profitable
flows.description: Jobs exist only when capital finds hiring profitable, which makes unemployment an artificial scarcity.

sources.note: We wait until capital decides it's profitable enough to hire.

flows.label: paves the way for profit
flows.description: A captured state uses its spending and policy to open up profitable opportunities for capital.

sources.note: The state's investments pave the way for profitability for capital.

flows.label: kept cheap: export more for less
flows.description: Blocked from sovereign development, Southern economies are held in subordinate supply-chain roles: they must export far more embodied labor and resources than they get back, a hidden transfer of value.

sources.note: Destroy their development and make them cheap once again.

sources.anchor: subordinate positions within global supply chains
sources.note: Structural adjustment pushed the South into subordinate positions in global supply chains.
Price inequalities produce a hidden transfer of value from South to North.

flows.label: extraction with impunity
flows.description: Having degraded its home ecological base, capital looks for an outside frontier where nature can be taken with impunity: no regulation, and dispossession of the people who depend on it.

sources.note: Exploiting the domestic ecological base runs into limits.
So capital needs an external frontier to take cheap nature from.
'Cheap' means extracting with impunity and dispossessing people.
Capitalism needs an outside where it can exploit with impunity and externalize its costs.

sources.anchor: ecological consequences are suffered in the periphery
sources.note: The benefits are consumed in the core; low wages and ecological damage stay in the periphery.

flows.label: damage lands on the South
flows.description: The atmosphere and ecosystems are shared, but the damage is not. Hickel calls this a double class dimension: the North causes most excess emissions (F7) while the South is most exposed, and even within the North it is working people who suffer most. The IPCC finds the same pattern (F10).

sources.anchor: Even as the world is burning
sources.note: Investment keeps going to fossil fuels even as the world burns.
Continuing this production will cause mass misery.
Working classes suffer climate impacts more, even in Northern countries.
The regions most vulnerable to climate impacts are overwhelmingly in the Global South.
The consequences of climate change fall along colonial lines.
The social and ecological costs land in places like the Congo, Indonesia and Brazil, not in the core.

flows.label: democratically ratified goals
flows.description: The vote now reaches the economy: people set the investment goals.

sources.anchor: public finance mechanism that can make
sources.note: Public finance invests toward democratically ratified objectives.
Where citizens’ assemblies were trialed in Europe, people deliberating moved toward a more human-centered, planet-centered economy.
Economic democracy brings investment and finance into alignment with democratically ratified objectives.

flows.label: currency issuance
flows.description: The state funds public goals directly by issuing currency. The constraint is real resources, not money.

sources.note: The state issues currency and can mobilize labor for what's needed.

sources.anchor: whoever controls the issuance of currency
sources.note: Whoever controls the issuance of currency controls what gets produced.
The state produces money; countries with monetary sovereignty can issue currency and invest in what they want.

flows.label: build-out
flows.description: Renewable capacity is built directly, without waiting for it to become profitable.

sources.note: China's public-finance route to renewables leadership.

flows.label: universal provision
flows.description: Guaranteed housing, healthcare, transit and the rest.

sources.note: Organize production to guarantee universal access to necessities.

flows.label: funds
flows.description: Public money hires people directly for socially necessary work.

sources.note: No reason not to hire workers directly through public finance.

flows.label: anyone can join
flows.description: A living wage, around 35 hours a week, with workplace democracy, which sets the bar private employers have to meet.

sources.note: It increases the bargaining power of labor.

flows.label: local budgets
flows.description: Decentralized down to the neighborhood.

sources.note: Public budgets allocated to local areas.

flows.label: national projects
flows.description: Centralized when the task needs it.

sources.note: National rail is decided centrally.

flows.label: decide locally
flows.description: The community decides what work it needs.

sources.note: Neighborhoods collectively decide what to invest work into.

flows.label: ground game
flows.description: Local organizing builds the base for a mass party.

sources.note: A strong ground game built on neighborhood associations.
Withstanding attacks takes organizing wall-to-wall solidarities in communities.

flows.label: wins power
flows.description: The party wins elections and takes democratic control of the state.

sources.anchor: building some kind of political machine
sources.note: A party that can win an election and implement change.

flows.label: workplace democracy
flows.description: Workers vote on what their workplace produces and how the yields are shared.

sources.note: Workers themselves decide.

flows.label: direct production
flows.description: Production follows the decisions of the people who do the work.

sources.note: What should we be producing, and for whose benefit?

flows.label: tax the rich
flows.description: Taxes don’t fund spending: a state with monetary sovereignty issues its own currency. Taxes reduce excess demand. So Hickel sees no reason to tax working-class incomes that don’t overconsume, and argues for a maximum income, a 100% tax above a democratically set threshold. This also shrinks the rich’s command over labor and resources and their power to corrupt democracy.

sources.anchor: reduce the demands of the rich
sources.note: Taxing the rich reduces their demands on our labor and productive capacity.
The real role of taxation is to reduce excess demand, not to fund spending.
A 100% tax above a threshold is a maximum income, and the threshold can be set democratically.
Hickel recommends a book he calls The Case for Maximum Income.

sources.anchor: purchasing power over real resources and labor
sources.note: Money is purchasing power over real resources and labor, so reducing the purchasing power of the rich is an ecological necessity.
Hickel recommends Gabriel Zucman's book as an account of how such a tax can be implemented and its negative consequences controlled.

flows.label: scale down
flows.description: Shrinking unnecessary industries frees real resources and keeps public production non-inflationary.

sources.note: Degrow unnecessary industries to free resources and avoid inflation.
Degrowth means scaling down damaging and unnecessary production, not all production.
A study Hickel’s team published found strong majority support in the US and UK for these proposals.

flows.label: sovereign development
flows.description: Southern states take control of their own resources and production.

sources.note: A functioning economy doesn't require imperialism; a capitalist one does.
sources.quote: a functioning economy, does not require imperialism. A capitalist economy does.

sources.note: To resolve these contradictions, the South has to break with constant accumulation and reclaim control over production.

flows.label: production for own needs
flows.description: Labor is organized around national development and human needs.

sources.note: Reclaiming control over productive capacity for human needs and national development.

flows.label: security
flows.description: Universal public services and guaranteed work end economic insecurity. People who are secure are less anxious and freer to take part, organize and innovate.

sources.note: The security of universal public services transforms people's lives.
With universal services people are happier and less anxious.

flows.label: community projects
flows.description: Local job budgets build what the community chose, such as a garden, a gym or elder care, which strengthens the associations that decided on them.

sources.note: Neighborhoods decide what work to invest in locally.

flows.label: yields shared
flows.description: In democratic workplaces, workers decide how what their labor yields is shared, instead of it flowing to capital as surplus.

sources.note: Workers decide how to distribute the yields of their own labor.
Sharing the surplus at Mondragon gives extremely low inequality inside the workplace.

flows.label: regeneration work
flows.description: Job guarantee work goes into restoring ecosystems, retrofitting and renewables: labor directed at repair instead of extraction.

sources.note: Job guarantee work includes regenerating ecosystems.
Public finance can invest in ecological regeneration.

flows.label: owns IP & tech
flows.description: Capital in the core owns the monopolies over intellectual property and high technology.

sources.note: Northern firms monopolize IP and high-tech production.

flows.label: monopoly prices
flows.description: Essential technologies and capital goods are sold to the South at monopoly prices.

sources.anchor: set the prices of those things very high
sources.note: Monopoly power lets the West set the prices of essential goods very high.

flows.label: Volcker shock & debt
flows.description: In 1980 the US Federal Reserve pushed interest rates above 20%, which broke organized labor at home and triggered a debt crisis across the South.

sources.note: The Volcker shock triggered a debt crisis across the Global South.
Sankara saw debt as an instrument of imperial control in the Global South.

flows.label: structural adjustment
flows.description: Loans conditioned on privatization, service cuts, abolishing industrial policy and limiting public finance, reversing the gains of the anti-colonial era.

sources.note: Structural adjustment forced privatization and cut public services.

sources.anchor: curtailed the ability of states to issue national currency
sources.note: It limited the use of national currency and public finance.

sources.anchor: labor rights are destroyed under structural adjustment
sources.note: Under structural adjustment, industrial policies are unwound, public services slashed and labor rights destroyed.

flows.label: oil priced in dollars
flows.description: Global oil and gas trade in dollars creates constant demand for the dollar.

sources.note: Everyone buys oil and gas in dollars.

flows.label: imperial privilege
flows.description: Constant demand for dollars lets the US import as much as it wants and run deficits.

sources.note: The petrodollar gives the US the privilege of importing freely and running deficits.

flows.label: defends fossil system
flows.description: Because its privilege rests on the petrodollar, the US state works to keep the fossil system alive as long as possible.

sources.anchor: trying to maintain the the fossil fuel system
sources.note: The US is heavily invested in maintaining the fossil fuel system.

sources.anchor: maintain uh the fossil fuel economy
sources.note: The capitalist class has strong reasons to maintain the fossil economy as long as possible.

flows.label: rising supply prices
flows.description: When Southern states produce and consume more for themselves, their resources stop being cheap: supply prices rise and core profits are pinched (the 1970s crisis).

sources.note: Sovereign development shows up as a rising supply price that destabilizes profits.
The rising supply price from the periphery caused inflation and stagnation in the core.

flows.label: squeeze
flows.description: As the rise of the South pinches profits, capital turns on its own working class: cutting wages and consumption at home.

sources.note: Capital is attacking its own working classes again.

sources.anchor: attacking consumption of the working class
sources.note: They try to maintain profitability by attacking working-class consumption.

flows.label: concessions (paid by empire)
flows.description: Under pressure from socialist revolutions abroad, capital made concessions to core workers (wages, welfare) and paid for them through cheap labor and resources from the South.

sources.anchor: dramatic concessions to their working classes
sources.note: Capital made dramatic concessions to Western working classes under revolutionary pressure.
Restoring the imperial arrangement let Europe keep its bargain with its workers.
A capitalist in Norway can concede to workers and get cheap labor elsewhere.
Scandinavia’s concessions depend on imperial privilege: cheap labor and resources from the periphery.

flows.label: anger captured
flows.description: Justified anger at elites, with no socialist movement to join, is drawn into the far right's anti-establishment rhetoric.

sources.note: Without a movement ready, anger flows to the far right.

flows.label: wins power
flows.description: The far right takes office and governs for the same capitalist class.

sources.note: The beneficiaries of these movements are the existing capitalist class.
Fascists take control.

flows.label: votes for the "safe center"
flows.description: After far-right chaos, voters return to the liberal center.

sources.note: Voters swing back to the liberals; rinse and repeat.

flows.label: keeps the seat warm
flows.description: Liberal governments leave the underlying contradictions untouched, and the next right-wing wave follows.

sources.note: Liberal parties keep the seat warm for the next right-wing party.

flows.label: chaos → backlash
flows.description: Far-right rule produces social chaos, pushing voters back toward the liberal center.

sources.note: The fascists create total social chaos and people retreat to the center.

flows.label: growth imperative
flows.description: Capital profits most by growing total output while keeping the working class’s share down, so it pushes for growth of anything, whatever it is.

sources.anchor: deny the working class as much
sources.note: Grow total output and deny the working class as much of it as possible.

sources.anchor: growth of what and for who
sources.note: The real question: growth of what, and for whom?

flows.label: heat hits workers
flows.description: Within the North too, heat waves and climate impacts hit working-class people hardest.

sources.note: Working classes suffer more from heat waves and climate effects.

flows.label: climate impacts hit hardest
flows.description: The regions most vulnerable to climate impacts are overwhelmingly in the Global South, where heat deaths are not even counted.

sources.note: The regions most vulnerable to climate impacts are overwhelmingly in the Global South.

sources.anchor: those deaths are not even counted
sources.note: Heat deaths in Global South countries are not even counted; think of a rickshaw driver in Delhi at 45°.

flows.label: fair-terms tech & trade
flows.description: Technology, producer goods and infrastructure on fairer terms, letting Southern states escape unequal exchange with the core.

sources.note: The Belt and Road gives the South access to technologies on more favorable terms.

flows.label: South–South trade
flows.description: Trading with each other through swap lines, outside the dollar and the euro, and cooperating on defense.

sources.anchor: swap lines outside of core currencies
sources.note: South–South trade and swap lines outside core currencies.
Swap lines with China and others bypass the dollar.

flows.label: pinches profits
flows.description: China's rising wages and its intrusion into Western monopolies both cut into core profits.

sources.note: Chinese labor is no longer cheap.
China's industrial development has intruded on Western monopolies.

flows.label: rules & quotas
flows.description: The democratic state sets lending rules and quotas for commercial banks.

sources.note: Credit guidance imposes rules on commercial banks.

flows.label: conversion: cars → solar
flows.description: Workers in control can convert their own factories toward socially useful production.

sources.note: Workers switched a car plant to producing solar panels.
Cargo bikes and solar panels instead of cars.

sources.anchor: parts for bikes and solar panels
sources.note: After an Italian car-parts firm closed, its workers reopened it making bike parts and solar panels.

flows.label: bargaining power
flows.description: With housing, healthcare and the basics guaranteed, workers can refuse exploitation, and the economy no longer needs perpetual growth to stay stable.

sources.anchor: increases the bargaining power of the working class
sources.note: Access to basics increases the bargaining power of the working class.
Universal services make the economy resilient without perpetual growth.

flows.label: own-currency finance
flows.description: Sovereign states finance development in their own currency instead of depending on foreign capital.

sources.note: Public finance in the national currency.

flows.label: public works & hiring
flows.description: Training and hiring the unemployed to build housing, clinics, sanitation and a sovereign industrial base.

sources.note: Hire people directly to achieve national development objectives.
Fund houses, schools, clinics and sanitation.

flows.label: development for own needs
flows.description: Southern labor and resources build hospitals, schools and sanitation for their own people instead of gadgets and fast fashion for the North.

sources.note: Production for their own hospitals, schools and sanitation systems.
Organize production around national development and human needs.

flows.label: quotas on bank lending
flows.description: Commercial banks may keep operating, but must align lending with democratically ratified goals instead of whatever is most profitable.

sources.anchor: imposes rules on the commercial banks
sources.note: Banks must meet quotas, e.g. for renewables or high-speed rail.
Limit finance to fossil fuels; steer it toward renewables.

flows.label: credit steered to renewables
flows.description: Under credit guidance, private bank credit flows to renewables and other necessary sectors.

sources.note: Credit guidance organizes investment toward the most necessary sectors.

flows.label: pressure outsourced
flows.description: One capitalist world economy: capital needs cheap labor and resources, so the pressure is placed on the periphery and the violence is outsourced there, not to the core.

sources.note: There is one capitalist world economy, with violence outsourced to the periphery so the pressure is not in the core.

sources.anchor: capital requires cheap labor and cheap resources
sources.note: Capital requires cheap labor and cheap resources to maximize profits.

flows.label: demands for better wages
flows.description: Workers in the periphery make the same demands as workers in the core: better wages and health care.

sources.anchor: if you're a capitalist in the periphery
sources.note: Capitalists in the periphery cannot concede to these demands the way those in the core can.

flows.label: violent repression
flows.description: Trade unionists are often murdered. Hickel presents this as what a capitalist economy in the periphery has no alternative but to do; he does not separate out who carries it out.

sources.note: Across the mostly capitalist South there is violent repression of social movements; trade unionists are often murdered.
In Eswatini, violence against trade unionists and protesters is constant.

flows.label: protesters repressed
flows.description: Huge amounts of violence against protesters, to the point where, in Hickel’s home country of Eswatini, politics is frozen.

sources.note: In Eswatini, violence against protesters leaves politics frozen.
The South is seen as corrupt and violent, but this is one world economy with its violence outsourced.

flows.label: land defenders attacked
flows.description: The violence falls on environmental defenders too. It happens in the mines of Congo, the mountains of the Andes and the forests of Indonesia.

sources.note: Environmental defenders are among those facing violent repression.
The violence happens in the mines of Congo, the Andes and the forests of Indonesia.

flows.label: liberation struggles
flows.description: Social progress in the periphery came with anti-colonial movements that kicked out the colonizers and regained control over land and resources. Resolving global inequality requires struggles for liberation from the South.

sources.anchor: struggles for liberation from the global south
sources.note: Resolving global inequality requires struggles for liberation from the South to reclaim resources and productive capacities.
Progress in the periphery began with anti-colonial movements regaining control over land and resources.

flows.label: demand lifts incomes
flows.description: Some improvements in the South since the commodities boom, as incomes rose on the back of demand from China.

sources.anchor: on the back of demand from China
sources.note: Incomes in the South have risen on the back of demand from China since the commodities boom.

flows.label: protest & organize
flows.description: People organize and take to the streets because they cannot stand by and watch; Hickel says they have to, even though it is not enough.

sources.note: People have to protest, because they cannot stand by without resisting.

flows.label: protest alone falls short
flows.description: Protest brings people out, but this generation has seen the limits of what it can deliver without political power.

sources.note: Simply protesting is not enough; political machines have to be built.

sources.anchor: limits to the extent to which
sources.note: The limits of protest have been revealed: it cannot deliver what people pin on it.

flows.label: repression
flows.description: People resisting the genocide in Gaza and the abandonment of climate action are met with repression, which Hickel calls madness, in the UK and the US.

sources.anchor: faced with this kind of repression
sources.note: People who want to resist are met with repression.

flows.label: smear campaigns
flows.description: When a left-populist figure breaks through, the media smear campaign ramps up. A movement tied to one person cannot withstand it, as with Corbyn.

sources.note: A figure without a mass party behind them is vulnerable when the media smear campaign ramps up.

flows.label: united in a mass party
flows.description: A mass party connects people across struggles toward shared objectives, by naming the common problem: the capitalist economy.

sources.note: A mass party can connect people across different struggles, united toward shared objectives.
A mass political party integrates different struggles into one machine with a chance at power.

flows.label: concessions won by struggle
flows.description: Public services, the weekend and workers’ votes had to be fought for against the interests of the capitalist class. Progress in the core began with labor and socialist movements in the late 19th century.

sources.anchor: they had to be fought for
sources.note: These gains had to be fought for against the interests of the capitalist class.

sources.anchor: rise of the labor movements and the socialist movements
sources.note: Progress in the core coincided with the rise of labor and socialist movements.
Revolutions forced capitalists in Western Europe to make major concessions.

flows.label: controls AI, for profit
flows.description: The people developing AI do not have our interests at heart, and we have no democratic control over it.

sources.anchor: do not have our interests at heart
sources.note: The people developing AI do not have our interests at heart.
Capital’s objective with any technology is to leverage it for more profit.

flows.label: jobs automated
flows.description: People watch their jobs being automated and are cut off. That is why AI is frightening in this system.

sources.note: People see their jobs being automated and are cut off.

flows.label: democratic say over AI
flows.description: In a more democratic socialist setting, people would have a say over how the technology is deployed, and much less reason to be afraid.

sources.anchor: democratic say over how this technology
sources.note: With a democratic say over how the technology is deployed, there is much less reason for concern.

flows.label: shorter working week
flows.description: If AI delivers reductions in labor time, the working week can shrink and necessary jobs can be shared, leaving everyone more leisure time.

sources.note: Reduced labor time could shorten the working week, with necessary jobs shared.

flows.label: labor freed for needed work
flows.description: Or labor is remobilized toward what actually needs doing: ecological restoration, care work and public transit.

sources.note: Labor can be remobilized toward things that are needed: ecological restoration, care work, public transit.

flows.label: resources & labor freed
flows.description: Reducing production of SUVs, mansions and private jets frees resources and labor to be redirected to what people need.

sources.note: Reducing damaging production liberates resources and labor for things that are actually needed.

flows.label: exit taxes & capital controls
flows.description: If the rich leave, they cannot take land or factories with them. The risk is selling the currency, which exit taxes like Norway’s, capital controls and minimum taxes across the EU or globally can deal with.

sources.note: People who leave cannot take productive capacities like land or factories with them.
Selling the currency can be dealt with through exit taxes, capital controls and shared minimum taxes.

flows.label: writes the rules
flows.description: Great powers create institutions and write their rules to serve their own interests, which makes institutions valuable instruments of statecraft. Mearsheimer’s account is about national interest; he does not tie it to capital.

sources.note: Institutions are valuable instruments of statecraft for great powers.

sources.anchor: they write the rules to serve
sources.note: Great powers write the rules to serve their interests.

flows.label: rules bind the weak
flows.description: Minor powers don’t write the rules and almost always have to obey them. The enforcer is not the institution, which has hardly any power, but the economic and military might of the great powers behind it. Mearsheimer adds that minor powers often benefit from the rules too.

sources.anchor: they have to obey the rules
sources.note: Minor powers have to obey the rules in almost all cases.

sources.anchor: the institution itself has hardly any power
sources.note: Enforcement comes from the great powers’ might, not from the institution.

flows.label: no consequences
flows.description: When rules conflict with a great power’s interest it breaks them, and no higher authority can punish it (Mearsheimer). Hickel makes the same observation from another angle: flagrant violations of international law bring zero consequences, which he calls a symptom of capitalist imperialism.

sources.note: A great power can disobey the rules it wrote, and no higher authority can punish it.
Flagrant violations of international law bring zero consequences.
Hickel calls this a symptom of a deeper pattern, capitalist imperialism.

flows.label: democratic majority
flows.description: Southern states organized in the G77 to act together in the UN, where they hold the majority. In 1974 they passed the New International Economic Order, establishing principles of national economic sovereignty.

sources.anchor: where they held a democratic majority
sources.note: The G77 held a democratic majority in the UN.
In 1974 they passed the NIEO, a massive win for Southern states.

flows.label: West moves to contain
flows.description: Western governments scrambled for a way to contain this insurgent South, and found it in the Volcker shock.

sources.anchor: scrambling for a way to contain
sources.note: Western governments scrambled to contain the insurgent South.

flows.label: uses IMF & World Bank
flows.description: The US leveraged the debt crisis by using the World Bank and IMF to impose structural adjustment across the South, reversing the policies of the anti-colonial era.

sources.anchor: by using the World Bank and the IMF
sources.note: The US used the World Bank and IMF to impose structural adjustment.

flows.label: majority stops here
flows.description: Nearly every state sits in the Assembly, but a great power on the Council can veto anything the UN wants to do that it finds unacceptable. This mirrors “votes stop at production”: a majority that does not reach where power sits. The parallel is our framing.

sources.note: Great powers on the Council can veto anything they find unacceptable.

flows.label: takes it to court
flows.description: A Southern state can bring another state before the court and ask for interim orders while the full case proceeds, which can take years.

sources.note: A state can ask the court to indicate provisional measures while a case proceeds.

flows.label: ruling doesn’t bind
flows.description: No international institution has significant coercive leverage over a great power (Mearsheimer). Law without institutions able to enforce it is fiction (Varoufakis). Applying this to the ICJ is our synthesis: Mearsheimer does not name the court.

sources.anchor: significant coercive leverage over the great powers
sources.note: No international institution has significant coercive leverage over the great powers.

sources.anchor: with institutions with the power to enforce
sources.note: Law without institutions with the power to enforce it is fiction.
sources.speaker: Varoufakis

flows.label: political pressure
flows.description: Finkelstein describes officials across the UN system as open to political pressure, with a top court the place where all the politics of the world reach their climax.

sources.anchor: susceptible to all sorts of political pressures
sources.note: People in the UN system are susceptible to all sorts of political pressures.
A top court is a condensation of world politics.

flows.label: selective backing
flows.description: Varoufakis: Western leaders celebrate some indictments and shrug off others, which is why he calls international law a “theater of hypocrisy”, founded on principles the West itself rarely honors.

sources.note: International law has been reduced to a theater of hypocrisy.
sources.speaker: Varoufakis

flows.label: fear of a trial
flows.description: Even if it is unenforced, the law instills fear: a small chance that a strongman who loses a war he started ends up in a Nuremberg-style trial. Varoufakis calls that fear not insignificant, which is a real difference from Mearsheimer’s view that nothing can punish a great power.

sources.note: Even a small probability of trial instills fear in strongmen.
sources.speaker: Varoufakis

sources.note: That fear is not insignificant.
sources.speaker: Varoufakis

flows.label: yardsticks for hypocrisy
flows.description: Agreed definitions of war crimes and genocide are yardsticks to measure leaders’ hypocrisy, and campaigners can quote rights back at their governments in UN processes. So the law gives movements something to use even when it isn’t enforced.

sources.note: These definitions are yardsticks for measuring leaders’ hypocrisy, essential for agitating.
sources.speaker: Varoufakis

sources.note: Campaigners get something they can quote back in their own societies.
sources.speaker: Corbyn

flows.label: public opinion constrains
flows.description: Shared norms shape what is seen as acceptable, and through politics and public opinion they constrain even strongmen (Varoufakis). Enforcement comes down to national parliaments and international opinion (Corbyn). Hickel stresses how far protest falls short without political power, so read this next to the blocked “protest alone falls short” arrow.

sources.anchor: The influence that public opinion has
sources.note: Public opinion influences even strongmen, and shared norms constrain them through politics.
sources.speaker: Varoufakis

sources.note: Pressure and enforcement come down to national parliaments and international opinion.
sources.speaker: Corbyn

flows.label: basis to act together
flows.description: The strongest may decide these laws don’t apply to them, but every other country needs them. They give weaker countries a legitimate basis to act together, through coalitions, sanctions or the courts (Maddox).

sources.anchor: legitimacy for other countries to act together
sources.note: The laws give other countries the legitimacy to act together.
sources.speaker: Maddox

sources.anchor: every other country that is not one of the strongest needs those laws
sources.note: Countries that are not the strongest need these laws, and know it.
sources.speaker: Maddox

flows.label: build a UN that can act
flows.description: Agitation can turn principles that perpetrators disobey and the righteous cannot enforce into a United Nations with the capacity to act. Varoufakis calls it a long process with no guarantee, and says the legacy must not be wiped out because it isn’t enforced. Hickel’s talks don’t say what these institutions become under Southern sovereignty.

sources.note: The aim is a United Nations with the capacity to act; a long process.
sources.speaker: Varoufakis

contrasts.question: Who decides investment?
contrasts.today: Capital, by profitability (the law of value)
contrasts.alt: A public finance mechanism, toward democratically ratified goals

sources.note: Profitability is the rule for investment.

sources.anchor: public finance mechanism that can make
sources.note: Public finance invests in what people vote for.
Planning already exists; it is just undemocratic.

contrasts.question: Where does the vote reach?
contrasts.alt: Politics and production: public finance goals, workplaces, neighborhood budgets

sources.note: No democracy in the system of production.
Workers decide in democratic firms.

contrasts.question: What gets produced?
contrasts.today: Whatever is most profitable: luxuries overproduced, necessities short
contrasts.alt: What is socially and ecologically necessary, with universal access

sources.note: Overproduction of luxuries, shortages of necessities.
A decommodified social foundation.

contrasts.question: Unemployment
contrasts.today: A constant threat that disciplines workers
contrasts.alt: Abolished by a public job guarantee

sources.note: The threat of unemployment keeps workers subordinate.
The public job guarantee.

contrasts.question: How is spending kept non-inflationary?
contrasts.today: Not posed as a choice: capital commands labor through money
contrasts.alt: Tax the rich and scale down unnecessary industries to free real resources

sources.note: Money is command over labor.
Degrow unnecessary industries to avoid inflation.

contrasts.question: North–South relations
contrasts.today: Appropriation of cheap labor and nature, enforced by force and debt
contrasts.alt: Sovereign development; no imperial arrangement needed

sources.note: Core growth depends on appropriation from the South.
A functioning economy doesn't require imperialism.
A second stage of decolonization.

contrasts.question: Ecosystem
contrasts.today: Growth-driven extraction and emissions; efficiency gains eaten by growth
contrasts.alt: Total energy and material use falls in rich countries

sources.note: Efficiency gains wiped out by growth.
Scale down total energy use.

contrasts.question: Scale of decisions
contrasts.alt: At the fitting level: neighborhood budgets, national projects, global sovereignty

sources.note: A small elite controls production.
Decentralized to neighborhoods where it fits.
Centralized for national rail.

loops.label: Accumulation loop
loops.description: Capital invests where profit is highest, those sectors pay it back with more, and the larger pool of capital is invested by the same rule. Luxuries keep growing while necessities stay short.

sources.note: Profitability is the investment rule.
Luxuries are overproduced; necessities are short.

loops.label: Fossil lock-in loop
loops.description: Fossil fuels pay 3–4× more than renewables, so their profits keep refinancing fossil fuels, even though renewables are cheaper and the planet is burning.

sources.anchor: three or four times more profitable
sources.note: Fossil fuels are 3–4× more profitable.
BlackRock drops climate goals: not profitable enough.

loops.label: Discipline loop
loops.description: Workers' labor creates the surplus that capital controls. Capital decides who gets hired, and the fear of unemployment keeps workers producing that surplus on capital's terms.

sources.note: The surplus comes from our labor.
The threat of unemployment keeps workers subordinate.

loops.label: State capture loop
loops.description: Capital captures the state, and the state uses public spending and policy to make capital more profitable, which increases its power to capture the state.

sources.note: The state is captured by capital.
State investment paves the way for profit.

loops.label: Consent loop
loops.description: Billionaire-owned media make 'capitalism = freedom' common sense. People vote within that common sense, and the governments they elect keep serving capital.

sources.note: Billionaires own the press.
'Capitalism is freedom' is cultural hegemony.

loops.label: War profits loop
loops.description: A captured state spends heavily on the military, the weapons industry's profits flow to capital, and capital's influence over the state grows.

sources.note: Public money goes to the military, not public services.
The weapons industry channels surplus to billionaires.

loops.label: Imperial drain loop
loops.description: Core growth depends on cheap labor from the South. When Southern states try sovereign development, force makes them cheap again, the drain resumes, and the surplus flows back to capital in the core.

sources.note: Sovereign development gets attacked.
…to make them cheap once again.
Core growth depends on appropriation from the South.

loops.label: Debt & structural adjustment loop
