loops.description: The Volcker shock turned Southern debt into a crisis; the IMF and World Bank used it to impose structural adjustment, re-cheapening Southern labor and resources, and the drain resumed, rescuing profits in the core.

sources.note: The Volcker shock triggered the Southern debt crisis.

sources.anchor: mechanism for restoring the imperial arrangement
sources.note: Neoliberalism restored the imperial arrangement.
Sankara: debt as an instrument of imperial control.

loops.label: Cost-shifting loop
loops.description: Profitable fossil investment heats the shared atmosphere. The damage lands mostly on the South, while the South's land and resources keep being drained to fuel the next round of accumulation. Benefits flow North; costs flow South.

sources.anchor: Even as the world is burning
sources.note: Investing in fossil fuels even as the world burns.
Nature taken with impunity, people dispossessed.

loops.label: Frontier loop
loops.description: With its home ecological base degraded, capital reaches for an outside frontier of cheap nature. What it extracts there feeds production and returns as surplus, financing the next push outward.

sources.note: The domestic ecological base becomes degraded.
Capital needs an external frontier.

loops.label: Democratic investment loop
loops.description: People vote on investment goals, public finance delivers universal necessities, and the security that follows frees people to take part in deciding the next round.

sources.anchor: public finance mechanism that can make
sources.note: Public finance invests in what people vote for.
Security from universal public services.

loops.label: Local democracy loop
loops.description: Neighborhood organizing builds a party that wins power. The state funds a job guarantee whose local budgets are decided in the neighborhood, and the projects they build strengthen the neighborhood associations.

sources.note: Ground game through neighborhood associations.
Job guarantee decentralized to neighborhoods.

loops.label: Workplace democracy loop
loops.description: Workers decide what their workplace produces, and they decide how the yields are shared, so what labor creates comes back to the people who did the work.

sources.note: Democracy in the workplace.
Workers decide how to distribute the yields.

loops.label: Unequal exchange loop
loops.description: Core capital owns the monopolies and sells technology dear; to pay, the South must export far more embodied labor than it gets back. The difference returns to the core as surplus, which deepens the monopolies.

sources.anchor: set the prices of those things very high
sources.note: Monopoly prices force the South to export more.
The South exports many times more embodied labor than it imports.

loops.label: Petrodollar loop
loops.description: Oil traded in dollars props up US imperial privilege, so the US state defends the fossil system, which keeps oil, and the dollar, at the center.

sources.note: The petrodollar is a pillar of US imperial privilege.

sources.anchor: trying to maintain the the fossil fuel system
sources.note: So the US works to maintain the fossil system.

loops.label: Growth treadmill loop
loops.description: Growth is capital’s easiest route to profit, and profit funds the next push for growth: more output of anything, more pressure on energy systems and the biosphere.

sources.anchor: deny the working class as much
sources.note: Grow output, keep workers’ share down.

sources.anchor: growth of what and for who
sources.note: Growth of what, and for whom?

loops.label: Sovereignty pinch loop
loops.description: A balancing loop that holds the system in place. When the South develops for itself, supply prices rise and core profits are pinched; capital, through the state, answers with coups and wars that push the South back down.

sources.note: Sovereign development raises supply prices.
The core chose to restore the imperial arrangement.

sources.anchor: triggering uh economic crisis in the core
sources.note: Southern sovereignty triggered crisis in the core.

loops.label: Squeeze → far right loop
loops.description: When force can no longer keep the South cheap, the pinch moves inward: capital squeezes its own workers, their anger is captured by the far right, and a far-right state keeps serving capital.

sources.anchor: pinched off by the rise of the south
sources.note: Profits pinched by the rise of the South.
Without an alternative, the result is fascism.

loops.label: Liberal–far-right cycle
loops.description: Liberals leave control over production untouched, the far right rises, its chaos sends voters back to the "safe center", and the cycle repeats. Capital wins either way.

sources.note: Rinse and repeat.
Liberals keep the seat warm for the right.

loops.label: Imperial bargain loop
loops.description: Concessions to core workers keep them producing and consenting, and they are paid for out of a surplus swollen by the South's drained labor. This loop shares its surplus arrow with the Imperial drain, Unequal exchange and Debt loops.

sources.anchor: dramatic concessions to their working classes
sources.note: Concessions to Western workers…
…sustained by restoring the imperial arrangement.

loops.label: South–South loop
loops.description: Southern states trade, finance and defend each other outside core currencies, which deepens their sovereignty. Already emerging today through China, the Belt and Road and swap lines; in a world of Southern sovereignty it becomes the norm.

sources.note: Already under way: fair-terms access to technology.

sources.anchor: swap lines outside of core currencies
sources.note: South–South trade and swap lines.
South–South solidarity and defense alliances are essential.

loops.label: Sovereign development loop
loops.description: Own-currency finance hires the unemployed to build what the country needs, and that development strengthens the state’s sovereignty to do more.

sources.note: Finance development in your own currency.
Produce hospitals, schools and sanitation for your own people.

loops.label: Outsourced violence loop
loops.description: Capital’s need for cheap labor puts pressure on the periphery, repression keeps labor cheap there, and its product returns to the core as surplus. The core looks peaceful because the violence happens somewhere else.

sources.note: The violence is outsourced to the periphery.
In the core, capital can make concessions and things seem fine because the violence happens elsewhere.

loops.label: Periphery repression loop
loops.description: Workers in the periphery demand better wages. With nowhere else to find cheap labor, capital there suppresses the demands.

sources.anchor: if you're a capitalist in the periphery
sources.note: There is no elsewhere for a capitalist in the periphery, so the demands cannot be met.

loops.label: Liberation loop
loops.description: People’s struggles win back control over land, resources and production, and states organize production around their needs. Progress in the periphery has come this way.

sources.note: Anti-colonial movements regained control and organized production around national development, housing and public services.

loops.label: Mass party loop
loops.description: Struggles unite in a mass party, which wins power and uses public finance to provide what people need, and that security builds the support the party stands on.

sources.anchor: robust support from the working classes
sources.note: Real mass parties need broad leadership and robust support from the working classes.

loops.label: Automation discipline loop
loops.description: Capital controls AI and deploys it for profit; jobs get automated, the threat of unemployment disciplines those still working, and their labor feeds capital’s surplus. This chain is our synthesis of Hickel’s points on AI and on unemployment.

sources.note: People see their jobs being automated.
The threat of unemployment keeps workers subordinate.

loops.label: Rules for the weak
loops.description: The North’s state writes the rules, and they bind Southern states. The South stays cheap, the surplus reaches capital, and capital holds the state that writes the rules. Mearsheimer explains the first half by national interest and Hickel the second by capital; joining them is our synthesis.

sources.anchor: they write the rules to serve
sources.note: Great powers write the rules to serve their interests.

sources.anchor: they have to obey the rules
sources.note: Minor powers have to obey them.

loops.label: Veto shield
loops.description: Because a great power can’t be punished, war spending carries no legal cost, arms profits flow to capital, and capital holds the state. Hickel says the violations bring zero consequences and reflect capitalist imperialism; the link through the veto comes from Mearsheimer, and the chain is our synthesis.

sources.anchor: set up to protect great powers
sources.note: The Council protects great powers from decisions they don’t like.
Flagrant violations of international law bring zero consequences.

loops.label: Majority stops at the door
loops.description: The South wins by majority in the UN, the West moves to contain it, and debt and structural adjustment undo the gains. This chain is Hickel’s own account of the 1970s and 1980s. The veto beside it, stopping the majority from reaching the Council, is Mearsheimer’s.

sources.anchor: where they held a democratic majority
sources.note: The G77 held a democratic majority in the UN.

sources.anchor: scrambling for a way to contain
sources.note: Western governments scrambled to contain the South.

loops.label: Court without teeth
loops.description: A Southern state goes to court, the ruling doesn’t bind a great power, and the pressure on the South continues. It runs through a blocked arrow on purpose: the route is open to try but doesn’t arrive. This chain is our synthesis of Mearsheimer, Finkelstein and Varoufakis.

sources.note: A state can seek provisional measures from the court.

sources.anchor: significant coercive leverage over the great powers
sources.note: No institution has significant coercive leverage over the great powers.

loops.label: The weak act together
loops.description: The counter-current: weaker states use the UN and its laws as a legitimate basis for acting together, and that gives them more to act on. Maddox argues the first part from the laws of war and Hickel the second from the G77; joining them is our synthesis.

sources.anchor: legitimacy for other countries to act together
sources.note: The laws give other countries the legitimacy to act together.
sources.speaker: Maddox

sources.anchor: where they held a democratic majority
sources.note: The G77 acted together through its UN majority.

loops.label: Yardsticks
loops.description: Agreed definitions give movements a way to expose hypocrisy; that agitation is what could turn the UN into something with the capacity to act. Varoufakis’s argument for keeping a law that isn’t enforced.

sources.note: Definitions are yardsticks, essential for agitating.
sources.speaker: Varoufakis

sources.note: The aim is a UN with the capacity to act.
sources.speaker: Varoufakis

events.label: Chinese Revolution
events.description: Expelled the imperial powers; Hickel says the US never forgave it.

sources.note: China's revolution as an example of breaking free from imperial arrangements.

events.label: Coup against Mosaddegh (Iran)
events.description: Iran's popular prime minister sought national control of its oil and was deposed in a US–UK coup, then replaced by the Shah.

sources.note: Mosaddegh was progressive and popular.
Regaining national control of oil triggered the coup.
Mosaddegh deposed in 1953.

events.label: Vietnam War
events.description: Framed in the interview as crushing a popular movement for peasant control of land and production.

sources.note: Popular socialist movements had to be violently crushed.

events.label: 1970s crisis
events.description: Southern liberation struggles strained capital accumulation, and the North faced a fork: accept decolonization or reimpose empire.

sources.note: The crisis came in the 1970s and may be returning now.

events.label: Assassination of Thomas Sankara (Burkina Faso)
events.description: Called for collective African debt cancellation, and was killed months later in a French-backed coup.

sources.note: Revolutionary leader of Burkina Faso in the 1980s.
Debt as imperial control; a call for collective cancellation.

events.label: Iraq, Afghanistan, Libya, Syria
events.description: Cited as wars waged by core economies within Hickel's lifetime.

sources.note: Wars by so-called liberal democracies.

events.label: Israel / Palestine
events.description: Hickel argues that US support since the 1960s has served to counter pan-Arab and socialist movements in the region.

sources.note: The occupation is connected to capitalist imperialism.
Israel used to destabilize radical movements in the region.

events.label: Sahel states & defense alliance
events.description: A current example of Southern states trying to break free from imperial arrangements.

sources.note: Seen right now in the Sahel countries.
Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger: defense alliances to deter backlash.

events.label: Colonial plunder (silver, sugar, cotton)
events.description: Colonial silver, sugar and cotton fueled Europe’s rise; cheap sugar even lowered European workers’ subsistence costs and wages.

sources.note: Cheap colonial sugar fed Europe’s working classes and kept wages down.
For most of the world’s majority, the first encounter with capitalism was at the end of a gun.

events.label: India turned into a raw-material exporter
events.description: Colonial trade deliberately converted India from a manufacturing country into an exporter of raw produce.

sources.note: India was converted from manufacturing to exporting raw produce.

events.label: Colonial mortality crisis in India
events.description: Hickel cites around 50 million excess deaths under British rule.

sources.note: Around 50 million excess deaths under British colonialism.

events.label: Russian Revolution as an anti-colonial break
events.description: A low-wage raw-material periphery broke with the imperial arrangement and industrialized rapidly.

sources.note: The Russian Revolution as an anti-colonial revolution.

events.label: Coup against Árbenz (Guatemala)
events.description: Western-backed coup.

sources.note: Árbenz deposed in 1954.

events.label: Lumumba deposed (Congo)
events.description: Western-backed coup.

sources.note: Lumumba deposed in 1961.

events.label: Coup against Goulart (Brazil)
events.description: Western-backed coup.

sources.note: Goulart deposed in 1964.

events.label: Coup against Nkrumah (Ghana)
events.description: Western-backed coup.

sources.note: Nkrumah deposed in 1966.

events.label: Sukarno ousted (Indonesia)
events.description: Western-backed coup.

sources.note: Sukarno deposed in 1967.

events.label: Coup against Allende (Chile)
events.description: Western-backed coup.

sources.note: Allende deposed in 1973.

events.label: New International Economic Order
events.description: The G77 used its UN majority to declare principles of national economic sovereignty.

sources.note: The NIEO established principles of economic sovereignty.

events.label: Volcker shock → Southern debt crisis
events.description: US interest rates above 20% broke labor at home and triggered the debt crisis abroad.

sources.note: The Volcker shock.

events.label: Structural adjustment era
events.description: Privatization, service cuts and the end of industrial policy across the South; incomes collapsed even as production rose.

sources.note: Structural adjustment programs.
Southern incomes deflated as prices were cheapened.
The neoliberal backlash pushed the South back into subordinate positions in global supply chains.

events.label: South Korea & Taiwan allowed industrial policy
events.description: The exception that proves the rule: supported as a cordon around China.

sources.note: Korea and Taiwan were allowed state-led industrial policy.

events.label: China: opening, then sovereign industrial policy
events.description: Opened to the West for technology, then used industrial policy and public finance to climb the technology ladder; wages rose many times over.

sources.note: Chinese wages rose sharply.

events.label: Sanctions on socialist states
events.description: Almost every socialist government was sanctioned soon after it formed.

sources.anchor: sanctioned almost all of the socialist governments
sources.note: Sanctions followed almost every socialist revolution.

events.label: Enclosure in England
events.description: After the Black Death, revolts abolished serfdom and built a more egalitarian society. Hickel describes capitalism as the backlash: elites enclosed the land, dispossessed peasants and turned them into wage laborers.

sources.note: Revolts after the Black Death succeeded in abolishing serfdom and feudalism.
Capitalism was historically a backlash against the revolutions that destroyed feudalism.
Hickel cites his team’s research: with the rise of capitalism from the long 16th century, human welfare declined across several key indicators.

events.label: Labor & socialist movements win gains
events.description: Progress in the core began here: affordable housing, public services and sanitation dramatically raised working-class living conditions and life expectancy.

sources.anchor: rise of the labor movements and the socialist movements
sources.note: Progress in the core coincided with labor and socialist movements.

events.label: Anti-colonial movements bring progress
events.description: Social progress in the periphery began as anti-colonial movements regained control over land and resources and organized production around national development, housing and public services.

sources.note: Progress in the periphery began with the anti-colonial movements.

events.label: Credit guidance & public finance in Europe
events.description: Governments told commercial banks what they could and could not fund. These tools were hollowed out from the 1980s, with the defeat of labor movements.

sources.note: Governments imposed rules on commercial banks in the mid-20th century.
These tools have been hollowed out since the 1980s under neoliberalism.

events.label: Commodities boom on Chinese demand
events.description: After the immiseration of structural adjustment, there have been some improvements as incomes rose on the back of demand from China.

sources.anchor: on the back of demand from China
sources.note: Incomes have risen on the back of demand from China.

explainers.title: Cheaper isn't enough: the law of value
explainers.intro: Renewables now produce electricity more cheaply than fossil fuels, yet investment keeps flowing into fossil fuels. Hickel's explanation across his talks: under capitalism, investment follows profit, not price and not need. Pick a decision rule below and see which option wins.

cost.title: Renewables are cheaper
cost.text: Wind and solar now generate electricity more cheaply than coal or gas.

sources.note: Renewables are cheaper than fossil fuels but less profitable.
Wind and solar are cheaper than electricity from coal or gas, yet the investment isn’t happening.
Renewables are cheaper than fossil fuels.
Fossil fuels are actually more expensive as an energy source.

profit.title: Fossil fuels are more profitable
profit.text: Hickel puts fossil fuels at roughly three to four times as profitable as renewables.

sources.anchor: three or four times more profitable
sources.note: Fossil fuels are three or four times more profitable.

sources.anchor: three or four times more profitable
sources.note: Three or four times more profitable.

sources.anchor: three to four times more profitable
sources.note: Around three to four times more profitable.
About three times more profitable.

rules.label: Lowest cost
rules.verdict: Renewables would win, which is why economists promised that falling prices would deliver a quick transition. It hasn't happened, because that isn't how investment decisions are made.

sources.note: Economists promised cheap renewables would deliver a quick transition; it’s not happening.

sources.anchor: on the basis of the sale price
sources.note: Capital doesn’t invest on the basis of sale price but of profit.

rules.label: Highest return to capital
rules.tag: Today: the capitalist law of value
rules.verdict: Fossil fuels win, and their profits refinance more fossil fuels: the Fossil lock-in loop. Necessary investments that pay less simply don’t get made.

sources.note: The capitalist law of value makes profitability the test for investment.

sources.anchor: three to four times more profitable
sources.note: So investment continues to flow to fossil fuels.
BlackRock: the green transition isn’t as profitable as dirty industry.

rules.label: Democratically ratified goals
rules.verdict: Renewables win: they’re built directly through public finance and credit guidance because they’re needed, whether or not they’re the most profitable option.

sources.anchor: public finance mechanism that can make
sources.note: Public finance invests toward democratically ratified objectives.
Credit guidance steers bank lending away from fossil fuels toward renewables.
Profitability is not a precondition for production.

reasons.title: Market structure: competition vs monopoly
reasons.text: Almost anyone can pool money and build a solar farm, so renewables are a competitive, low-margin market. Fossil fuels need huge up-front capital, which allows monopoly power, and capital prefers sectors where it can set prices.

sources.note: Renewables have low barriers to entry; fossil fuels are conducive to monopoly power.

reasons.title: Geopolitics: the petrodollar
reasons.text: Oil is traded in dollars, which underpins US imperial privilege. In a solar-powered world nobody would need dollars to buy energy, so the US state defends the fossil system.

sources.note: The petrodollar is a core pillar of US imperial privilege.

sources.anchor: in currencies that are not the US dollar
sources.note: Selling oil outside the dollar threatens Western capital accumulation.

reasons.title: Sunk capital: stranded assets
reasons.text: So much capital is already sunk into fossil infrastructure that phasing it out would mean big losses for its owners, so they keep it running as long as they can.

sources.note: Phasing out existing fossil infrastructure is a huge loss for the capitalist class that owns it.
Given the choice, capital builds mansions rather than insulating homes.
Public transit isn’t built because it isn’t profitable.
Capital flows to cruise ships over affordable housing.
Regenerative agriculture is chronically short because it is less profitable.

pairs.necessary: Cures for diseases of the poor

sources.note: Capital won’t develop cures for tropical diseases because the patients are poor.

sources.anchor: exploit cheap labor within global supply chains
sources.note: In the periphery, exploiting cheap labor is more profitable than investing in development.

cases.title: BlackRock walks back its green promise
cases.text: The world’s largest asset manager pledged green investment, then openly dropped it because the transition wasn’t profitable enough.

sources.note: BlackRock explicitly abandoned its climate rules.
“We’re abandoning this promise”: green isn’t as profitable as dirty industry.

cases.title: China: finance steered by national goals
cases.text: With public control over its financial system, China directs credit toward national development goals rather than maximum profit. Hickel says it now installs more renewable capacity each year than the rest of the world combined, and builds high-speed rail that Western commentators call unprofitable.

sources.anchor: public control over the financial system
sources.note: China is not constrained by the law of value in the same way: it controls its financial system.
China installs more renewable capacity each year than the rest of the world combined.

sources.anchor: profit is probably only number three
sources.note: A Chinese investment banker: profit is third or fourth on their list of priorities.

cases.title: Public healthcare
cases.text: Profitability is not a precondition for production: societies already build healthcare systems because they are needed, not because they pay.

sources.note: Profitability of any kind is not a precondition for production.
Spain builds a world-class healthcare system even though it isn’t profitable.

explainers.title: How the South is kept cheap
explainers.intro: Hickel's central claim: capitalism has always needed an outside, a periphery where labor and nature are cheap and costs can be dumped. Colonialism ended formally, but the drain did not. It now runs through three routes that all end in the same place: surplus for capital in the core.

why.title: Core consumption depends on it
why.text: About half of what the core consumes in materials and labor is net-appropriated from the South. Without that, the core would have to consume far less or extract far more at home.

sources.anchor: half of total consumption in the core
sources.note: Around half of core consumption is net-appropriated from the South.

why.title: The costs land in the South
why.text: The benefits are consumed in the North while the ecological and social damage happens in the periphery, the core mechanism of environmental injustice.

sources.note: The damage happens in the Congo, Indonesia and Brazil, not in the core.

sources.anchor: ecological consequences are suffered in the periphery
sources.note: Low wages and ecological damage stay in the periphery.

why.title: Catching up is ruled out
why.text: The income gap between core and periphery is wider than ever: catch-up development cannot happen while value flows from South to North.

sources.note: The core–periphery income gap is bigger than ever.
Catch-up is impossible under net South-to-North flows.

routes.title: Force
routes.text: States that try to use their own labor and resources for their own development are overthrown, bombed or sanctioned until they are cheap again.

sources.note: Any country that starts on sovereign development gets attacked.
Around 70 US regime-change operations in the Global South.

sources.anchor: Cold War was not about defeating socialism
sources.note: The Cold War was a campaign against economic sovereignty.

routes.title: Prices
routes.text: Southern wages and prices are held far below Northern ones, while the North sells technology at monopoly prices, so the South must export many times more embodied labor than it gets back.

sources.note: A hidden transfer of value from South to North.
The South exports many times more embodied labor than it imports.

sources.anchor: set the prices of those things very high
sources.note: Monopoly prices force the South to export more.

routes.title: Finance
routes.text: The Volcker shock turned debt into a crisis; structural adjustment then stripped Southern states of industrial policy and of the power to finance development in their own currency.

sources.note: The Volcker shock triggered the Southern debt crisis.

sources.anchor: curtailed the ability of states to issue national currency
sources.note: Structural adjustment limited national currency and public finance.

sources.anchor: whoever controls the issuance of currency
sources.note: Whoever controls currency controls what gets produced.

fork.title: The 1970s fork in the road
fork.text: By the 1970s the South was producing more for itself, so its labor and resources were no longer cheap. Rising supply prices and rising wages squeezed core profits, and the core faced a choice. Pick a path to see what it leads to on the map.

sources.note: The North could accept decolonization or reimpose the imperial arrangement.
A fork: accept decolonization and move beyond capitalism, or restore the arrangement.
The core governments faced a fork in the road.

options.label: Restore the imperial arrangement
options.text: What actually happened: coups against developmentalist governments, then the Volcker shock, debt and structural adjustment. Neoliberalism re-cheapened the South and rescued core profits.

sources.note: The core opted to restore the imperial arrangement.

sources.anchor: mechanism for restoring the imperial arrangement
sources.note: Neoliberalism restored the imperial arrangement.
It rescued capitalism in the core.

options.label: Accept decolonization
options.text: The road not taken: Southern sovereignty and decent wages at home, with an economy no longer organized around accumulation. Hickel argues this is still the way out, and that a functioning economy does not need empire.

sources.note: A functioning economy doesn’t require imperialism; a capitalist one does.

sources.anchor: post-capitalist transition in the global north
sources.note: Southern decolonization would force a post-capitalist transition in the North.

eras.label: Colonial plunder
eras.text: Capitalism rises on appropriation from the colonies.

eras.label: Liberation & development
eras.text: Revolutions and anti-colonial states reclaim production for their own needs.

eras.label: Counter-revolution
eras.text: Coups, wars and sanctions against sovereign development.

eras.text: Southern sovereignty pinches core profits; the fork in the road.

eras.label: Neoliberal restoration

eras.label: Today: empire under strain
eras.text: China’s rise, new wars, new Southern alliances.

program.title: Delink
program.text: Not autarky: breaking from exploitation by the core and from the world-scale law of value, so production serves national development.

sources.anchor: delink from the capitalist law of value
sources.note: Delinking from the capitalist law of value on a world scale.

program.title: Finance development in your own currency
program.text: Use public finance to build housing, clinics and sanitation, and to hire people capital leaves unemployed.

sources.note: A state that issues its own currency can finance its own development.
Hire the unemployed directly.

program.title: Industrial policy & import substitution
program.text: Build a sovereign industrial base and cut dependence on imports from the core and on core currencies.

sources.note: Use the industrial policy and planning strategies that worked in the 20th century.
Substitute imports with domestic production where possible.

program.title: South–South cooperation & defense
program.text: Trade through swap lines outside the dollar, and build defense alliances to deter the backlash.

sources.anchor: swap lines outside of core currencies
sources.note: South–South trade and swap lines.
Defense alliances, as Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger have formed.

explainers.title: One planet, unequal damage
explainers.intro: The atmosphere and the world's ecosystems are shared by North and South alike, but the use and the harm are not shared evenly. Hickel argues the crisis has a double class dimension: it is driven overwhelmingly by the rich countries and the classes who control production, and its consequences fall hardest on the Global South and on working people everywhere.

groups.label: Who causes it
groups.text: Growth-driven production pulls materials out of the ecosystem and pours emissions and waste back in, with fossil fuels and less-necessary production leading the way, and a frontier of cheap nature in the South.

sources.anchor: deny the working class as much
sources.note: Capital profits by growing total output.
Massive overuse of resources drives ecological breakdown.

groups.label: Who bears it
groups.text: The damage flows back unevenly: onto the Global South, and onto working-class people in the North who cannot buy their way out.

sources.note: A double class dimension to the crisis.

groups.label: What changes
groups.text: In Democratic socialism, unnecessary production is scaled down, finance is steered into renewables, factories are converted, and job guarantee work goes into regenerating ecosystems.

sources.note: Actively scaling down unnecessary forms of production.
Public investment in ecological regeneration.

bars.note: Shares of emissions above each country’s equal per-capita fair share, as of 2015.

bars.title: Responsibility for excess material use (beyond fair shares), 1970–2017
bars.note: Shares of material use above fair shares of a sustainable level.

exposure.title: The South is most exposed
exposure.text: Most Global South countries are still within their fair share of the carbon budget, yet a map of climate vulnerability is overwhelmingly a map of the Global South.

sources.note: Rich countries are responsible for about 90% of excess emissions.
The most vulnerable regions are overwhelmingly in the South.

exposure.title: Working people in the North too
exposure.text: Heat waves hit those in small flats without air conditioning, green space or affordable healthcare; the rich can retreat to air-conditioned comfort.

sources.note: Working classes suffer climate impacts more, even in the North.
The rich can retreat to their air-conditioned yachts.

dimensions.title: Between countries: atmospheric colonization
dimensions.text: Divide a safe carbon budget into equal per-person fair shares and the rich countries have massively overshot theirs. In doing so they have taken atmospheric space that belonged to everyone else, forcing others to cut faster. The consequences then fall along colonial lines.

sources.note: Divide the safe budget into per-capita fair shares for every country.

sources.anchor: forced to reduce their emissions faster
sources.note: Everyone else is forced to cut emissions faster.
The rich countries colonized the atmospheric commons.
The consequences fall along colonial lines.

dimensions.title: Within countries: class
dimensions.text: Responsibility tracks control over production and energy decisions, not individual choices; people cannot choose public transit that was never built, or products designed to last that are never made.

sources.note: The rich drive excess emissions; responsibility is deeply unequal.
Public transit isn’t built because it isn’t profitable.
Long-lasting products run against capital accumulation.

paradox.title: The paradox
paradox.text: World output already overshoots several planetary boundaries, yet billions of people lack healthy food, healthcare and decent housing. Hickel cites research from his group finding that decent living standards for everyone would need only a fraction of the energy and materials the world economy uses today. The problem is not scarcity but what the law of value chooses to produce.

sources.note: Aggregate resource and energy use overshoots several planetary boundaries.
Billions cannot access healthy food or necessary healthcare.
Decent living for all would need a fraction of current energy and materials.
Mass deprivation amid huge productive capacity.

energy.title: Rich countries must use less energy
energy.text: To decarbonize fast enough to stay within their fair shares, high-income countries have to reduce total energy use. Efficiency helps, but it is not enough on its own.

sources.note: High-income countries must scale down total energy use.
They need to reduce total energy use.
Efficiency improvements can achieve some of it.

energy.title: Growth eats efficiency
energy.text: Under a growth imperative, efficiency gains are wiped out by rising total use. AI’s promised energy savings turned into soaring demand from data centers.

sources.note: Efficiency gains are wiped out by growth in total use.

sources.anchor: growth of what and for who
sources.note: Growth of what, and for whom?

energy.title: Capital will not degrow
energy.text: Scaling down profitable but unnecessary production (SUVs, fast fashion, mansions, private jets) will not happen voluntarily, because no capitalist cuts a profitable line of business.

sources.note: Capital will never voluntarily cut profitable production.
Scaling down unnecessary forms of production.

alternative.title: Scale down what isn’t needed
alternative.text: Freeing labor and resources from SUVs, fast fashion and mansions makes room for what is needed, and keeps public spending non-inflationary.

sources.note: Degrow unnecessary industries to free resources.

alternative.title: Build what is needed, directly
alternative.text: Public finance and credit guidance put money into renewables, transit and retrofits whether or not they are the most profitable option.

sources.note: Steer credit away from fossil fuels and toward renewables.

alternative.title: Work that repairs
alternative.text: Job guarantee work regenerates ecosystems, and workers in control can convert their factories, from cars to solar panels.

sources.note: Job guarantee work includes regenerating ecosystems.
Workers converted a car plant to cargo bikes and solar panels.

alternative.title: Security without growth
alternative.text: Universal public services make the economy resilient, so it no longer needs perpetual growth just to keep people from losing their jobs and homes.

sources.note: Universal services make the economy resilient without perpetual growth.

explainers.title: Who decides what, and where
explainers.intro: Hickel's alternative is not one central plan. It is democracy at whatever level a decision belongs to: neighborhoods decide local work, workers decide what their firm makes, the nation decides strategic investment and public services, and the South decides its own development. Below, each decision shows who makes it in the world the switches currently describe. Flip a decision here and the map ripples.

principle.title: Decentralize by task
principle.text: A national high-speed rail network has to be planned centrally; beer, watches and chairs can come from democratically run firms in a market; local needs are best judged locally.

sources.note: Different forms of production need different levels of decentralization.
Everyday goods can come from democratized firms in a market.
National rail needs central decision-making.

levels.text: Where people live, organize and know what their community needs.

today.text: There is no local budget; whether people work depends on whether capital finds hiring them profitable.

sources.note: People wait until capital finds it profitable to hire them.

alt.text: A job guarantee budget the community allocates itself: a garden, a gym, elder care, a kids’ soccer team.

sources.note: Neighborhoods decide what work to invest in.

sources.note: Without a movement, anger goes to the far right.

sources.note: Neighborhood associations as the ground game.

levels.text: Where most people spend their working lives.

today.text: Owners decide what to produce, and the surplus workers create goes to capital.

sources.note: The surplus we create is reinvested without our say.

alt.text: Workers decide what to produce, how wages are set, and can convert the plant to useful production.

sources.note: Worker-owned firms set their own wage ratios.

sources.note: The threat of unemployment disciplines workers.

alt.text: The job guarantee sets the standard private employers have to match.

sources.note: The job guarantee raises labor’s bargaining power.

sources.note: Profitability is the investment rule.

figures.caveat: Not a Hickel source; he cites it at TEA 12:13. The authors find that economic elites and business groups have substantial independent influence and average citizens little or none. Majorities who disagree with elites or organized interests 'generally lose', but citizens often get what they want when they agree with elites, and majorities opposing a change usually get their way. The authors conclude for 'economic-elite domination' and 'biased pluralism'; 'oligarchy' appears only in their summary of another scholar's theory. Elites are proxied by the 90th income percentile. Disputed: Bashir (2015, Research & Politics) argues the test understates average citizens' influence and that they won about as often as elites when the two disagreed; Branham, Soroka & Wlezien (2017, Political Science Quarterly) also challenge it. Gilens and Page rejected these critiques in a 2016 reply.
